lessons.title: Current, potential difference and resistance
lessons.summary: Understand what current, potential difference and resistance really are, use Q = It and V = IR confidently, and read the I-V graphs of resistors, lamps and diodes.
objectives: I can calculate charge flow using Q = It and rearrange it to find current or time.
I can use V = IR to find potential difference, current or resistance.
I can describe the I-V characteristics of an ohmic conductor, a filament lamp and a diode.
I can explain how the resistance of a thermistor and an LDR changes with temperature and light.
I can describe how to investigate how the length of a wire affects its resistance.

activities.title: Charge and current
activities.content:
## What is electric current?

A metal wire is full of free electrons. On their own they drift about randomly. When a cell is connected, the electrons are pushed in one direction and we get a **current**.

**Current is the rate of flow of electric charge.** In other words, it tells you how much charge passes a point every second.

- Charge (**Q**) is measured in **coulombs (C)**.
- Current (**I**) is measured in **amperes / amps (A)**.
- Time (**t**) is measured in **seconds (s)**.

$Q = I \times t$

A current of 1 A means 1 coulomb of charge passes a point every second. That is a huge number of electrons (about 6 million million million!), which is why we count charge in coulombs rather than in electrons.

For current to flow you need two things:
1. A **closed loop** (a complete circuit with no gaps).
2. A **source of potential difference**, such as a cell or battery, to push the charge round.

In a single closed loop the current is the **same at every point**. Charge is never used up: the same number of electrons that leave the cell return to it.

activities.title: Worked example: using Q = It
activities.content:
**A torch bulb carries a current of 0.30 A for 2 minutes. How much charge flows through it?**

1. Convert time to seconds: 2 minutes = 2 × 60 = **120 s**.
2. Use the equation: $Q = I t = 0.30 \times 120$
3. $Q = $ **36 C**

**Now rearrange it. A charge of 900 C passes through a heater in 5 minutes. What is the current?**

1. Time = 5 × 60 = 300 s.
2. $I = \dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{900}{300}$
3. $I = $ **3 A**

The most common slip in the exam is forgetting to change minutes into seconds. Always do that conversion first and write it down.

question.text: A phone charger supplies a current of 1.5 A for 40 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows. Give your answer in coulombs.
question.hint: Change the time into seconds before you multiply.

activities.title: Potential difference and resistance
activities.content:
## Potential difference (voltage)

A cell gives the charge energy. **Potential difference (p.d.)** is the energy transferred per coulomb of charge that passes between two points. It is measured in **volts (V)**, and 1 V means 1 joule of energy per coulomb.

- A **voltmeter** measures p.d. and is connected **in parallel** across the component.
- An **ammeter** measures current and is connected **in series** with the component.

## Resistance

**Resistance** is how much a component opposes the flow of current. It is measured in **ohms (Ω)**. The greater the resistance, the smaller the current for the same p.d.

$V = I \times R$

| Quantity | Symbol | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Potential difference | V | volt (V) |
| Current | I | ampere (A) |
| Resistance | R | ohm (Ω) |

Why do wires have resistance? The moving electrons collide with the vibrating metal ions in the wire. Each collision slows the electron down and transfers energy to the wire, heating it. A longer wire means more collisions, so **resistance is directly proportional to length**. A thinner wire also has more resistance.

activities.title: Worked example: V = IR three ways
activities.content:
**1. A 12 Ω resistor carries a current of 0.5 A. What is the p.d. across it?**

$V = IR = 0.5 \times 12 = $ **6 V**

**2. A p.d. of 230 V across a kettle element gives a current of 10 A. What is its resistance?**

$R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{230}{10} = $ **23 Ω**

**3. A 9 V battery is connected across a 450 Ω resistor. Find the current.**

$I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{9}{450} = $ **0.02 A** (which is 20 mA)

When you rearrange, cover up the quantity you want in the triangle: V on top, I and R side by side underneath. Always state the unit with your final answer.

question.text:
A p.d. of 4.5 V is applied across a small motor. A charge of 27 C flows through it in 60 s.

(a) Calculate the current.

(b) Calculate the resistance of the motor. Give your answer in ohms.
question.hint: Find the current first with I = Q ÷ t, then use R = V ÷ I.

question.text: How should a voltmeter be connected to measure the potential difference across a lamp?
question.hint: A voltmeter compares the energy per coulomb at two points, one on each side of the lamp.
question.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component so it measures the difference in potential between the two ends. An ammeter goes in series.

options.feedback: That is how an ammeter is connected.

options.text: In series with the cell only
Anywhere in the circuit, it makes no difference

activities.title: I-V characteristics
activities.content:
## Current-potential difference graphs

An **I-V characteristic** is a graph of current against potential difference for a component. Its shape tells you how the resistance behaves.

**Ohmic conductor (fixed resistor at constant temperature)**
- A **straight line through the origin**.
- Current is **directly proportional** to p.d.
- Resistance is **constant**. Doubling V doubles I.

**Filament lamp**
- A curve that gets **flatter** as V increases (an S-shape through the origin).
- As current increases the filament gets **hotter**, the metal ions vibrate more and the electrons collide more often.
- So **resistance increases** with temperature. Each extra volt gives a smaller increase in current.

**Diode**
- Current flows in **one direction only**.
- In the forward direction the current is almost zero until about 0.7 V and then rises steeply.
- In the reverse direction the resistance is **very high**, so the current is practically zero.

To obtain these graphs you use a **variable resistor** to change the current, record I and V, then reverse the cell to get the negative values. Switch off between readings so the components do not overheat.

activities.title: Worked example: reading an I-V graph
activities.content:
A student records these values for a component:

| p.d. (V) | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 4.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Current (A) | 0.50 | 0.80 | 1.00 | 1.15 |

**Is the component ohmic? Find its resistance at 1.0 V and at 4.0 V.**

- At 1.0 V: $R = V/I = 1.0 / 0.50 = $ **2.0 Ω**
- At 4.0 V: $R = 4.0 / 1.15 = $ **3.5 Ω**

The resistance is **not constant**, so it is **not ohmic**. The current rises by less and less for each extra volt, and the resistance grows as the component warms up. This is typical of a **filament lamp**.

Notice the key trap: on an I-V graph the resistance is **V divided by I at that point**, not the gradient of the curve.

question.text: Match each component to the description of its I-V characteristic.
question.hint: Think about which component only lets current through one way, and which one heats up.
question.explanation: A fixed resistor gives a straight line through the origin (constant resistance). A filament lamp gives a curve that flattens as it heats up. A diode only conducts in one direction.

pairs.right: Curve that becomes flatter as p.d. increases
Current flows in one direction only

activities.title: Thermistors, LDRs and the wire practical
activities.content:
## Components whose resistance changes

**Thermistor**: resistance **decreases as temperature increases**. Used in thermostats, fridges and car engine temperature sensors.

**Light-dependent resistor (LDR)**: resistance **decreases as light intensity increases**. In the dark its resistance is very high. Used in automatic street lights and camera light meters.

Both can be used in sensing circuits: as their resistance changes, the current in the circuit changes, which switches something on or off.

## Required practical: resistance and length of a wire

1. Tape a metre ruler to the bench and fix a length of thin resistance wire along it.
2. Connect the wire in series with a cell, a switch and an **ammeter**. Connect a **voltmeter** across the wire between the fixed end and a crocodile clip.
3. Move the clip to different lengths (10 cm, 20 cm ... 100 cm). Record V and I each time.
4. Calculate $R = V / I$ for each length.
5. Plot **resistance against length**: you get a straight line through the origin, so resistance is **directly proportional** to length.

**Controls and accuracy**: keep the current small and switch off between readings so the wire does not heat up (heating would raise its resistance). Use the same wire thickness throughout. Repeat and take a mean.

question.text: True or false: as the light shining on an LDR gets brighter, its resistance increases.
question.hint: Think about a street light that must switch OFF when it gets bright.
question.explanation: False. The resistance of an LDR falls as light intensity increases. In darkness its resistance is very high.

question.text:
A student plots the I-V characteristic of a filament lamp. The graph curves so that it becomes less steep as the potential difference increases.

(a) Describe what the shape of the graph shows about the resistance of the lamp as the p.d. increases. (1 mark)

(b) Explain, in terms of particles, why the resistance changes in this way. (3 marks)
question.hint: What happens to the temperature of the filament as more current flows, and what do the metal ions do when they are hotter?
question.explanation: (a) The resistance increases as p.d. increases because each extra volt produces a smaller increase in current. (b) A larger current makes the filament hotter; the metal ions vibrate more; the electrons collide with the ions more often, so it is harder for charge to flow and the resistance rises.

markScheme.criterion: States that resistance increases as p.d. (or current) increases
Current heats the filament / temperature increases
Electrons collide more often with the ions, making it harder for charge to flow

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Current** is the rate of flow of charge: $Q = It$ (charge in C, current in A, time in **seconds**).
- **Potential difference** is energy per coulomb, measured in volts. Voltmeters go in **parallel**, ammeters in **series**.
- $V = IR$. Resistance is in ohms (Ω) and grows with wire length.
- **Ohmic conductor**: straight line through the origin, constant R. **Filament lamp**: curve flattens as it heats up, R increases. **Diode**: current one way only.
- **Thermistor**: R falls as temperature rises. **LDR**: R falls as light gets brighter.
- Wire practical: R is directly proportional to length; keep the current low so the wire stays cool.

practiceQuestions.text: A current of 2 A flows for 30 s. Calculate the charge that flows, in coulombs.
A charge of 180 C passes through a lamp in 3 minutes. Calculate the current in amps.
practiceQuestions.hint: Convert 3 minutes to seconds first, then I = Q ÷ t.

practiceQuestions.text: A resistor of 220 Ω is connected to a 6 V battery. Calculate the current through it. Give your answer in amps to 3 decimal places.
A heater has a resistance of 46 Ω and takes a current of 5 A. Calculate the potential difference across the heater.
Which statement about an ohmic conductor is correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Ohmic means it obeys Ohm's law at constant temperature.
practiceQuestions.explanation: For an ohmic conductor current is directly proportional to p.d., so its resistance stays constant and the I-V graph is a straight line through the origin.

options.text: Current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature
Its resistance increases as the current increases
It only allows current in one direction
Its resistance falls as it gets brighter

metadata.blanksText: Charge is measured in ___, potential difference is measured in ___ and resistance is measured in ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: C, V and Ω are the symbols.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Charge: coulombs (C). Potential difference: volts (V). Resistance: ohms (Ω).

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of the following would increase the resistance of a piece of wire?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how often electrons collide with ions.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A longer wire and a hotter wire both increase resistance. A thicker wire has more room for electrons so its resistance is lower. Cooling reduces ion vibration and lowers resistance.

practiceQuestions.text: Put the steps of the wire resistance practical in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: You need readings before you can calculate anything.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Set up the circuit, choose a length, record V and I, calculate R = V ÷ I, then plot R against length.
order: Connect the wire in series with an ammeter and put a voltmeter across it
Clip the wire at a chosen length and close the switch
Record the readings on the voltmeter and ammeter
Calculate resistance using R = V ÷ I
Plot a graph of resistance against length

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why the current should be kept low and the switch opened between readings when investigating the resistance of a wire.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does a large current do to the wire, and how does that affect the variable you are measuring?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A large current heats the wire. A hotter wire has a higher resistance, so the results would no longer show only the effect of length.

markScheme.criterion: A large current would heat the wire / raise its temperature
Higher temperature increases resistance so results would be inaccurate / unfair

practiceQuestions.text:
A thermistor is used in a circuit that switches on a heater when a greenhouse becomes cold.

(a) Describe how the resistance of a thermistor changes with temperature. (1 mark)

(b) The thermistor is connected to a 12 V supply. At 20 °C the current is 0.020 A. Calculate its resistance at this temperature. (2 marks)

(c) State what happens to the current in the circuit when the temperature drops to 5 °C, and give a reason. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: Use R = V ÷ I for part (b). For (c) think about what a higher resistance does to current.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Resistance decreases as temperature increases. (b) R = 12 ÷ 0.020 = 600 Ω. (c) The current decreases because the resistance of the thermistor rises when it is colder.

markScheme.criterion: Resistance decreases as temperature increases (or increases as it gets colder)
Current decreases because resistance is higher at low temperature
